title: Read the question before you answer it
subtitle: Before you write a word, what exactly is this question asking for?
subject: Chemistry and Biology
lessonIntent: the routine (verb, marks, content words and givens, constraint, then tick each part); the meanings of "in terms of", "with reference to" and "using the information"; "one mark, one idea" with its three limits; two drills.

voiceover.text: Here's something NESA's marking feedback raises every year. In every HSC Chemistry and Biology report from 2020 to 2025, it points out answers that missed what the question actually asked. Often the student knew the science. They just answered a nearby question. So this video is about the step before you write anything: reading the question properly, in about thirty seconds.

Here's an HSC-style question. It gives an equilibrium: iron three plus ions join thiocyanate ions to make a red ion. A few crystals of iron three nitrate dissolve in the tube, the temperature stays the same, and the solution turns a deeper red. Then it asks you to explain the colour change, in terms of collision theory. Three marks. Before you answer, let's pull it apart.

Start with the verb. It tells you what to do with what you know. Here it's explain. NESA's glossary describes explain as showing cause and effect: how or why something happens. So a list of facts won't do. Your answer has to show why the colour changes. NESA also says to read every key word in the context of its question, and the next video is all about this one.

Next, the marks. Three marks tells you roughly how much the markers expect: about three linked points, which usually fits the lines you're given. It also tells you when to stop. Ten lines on everything you know about equilibrium won't earn a fourth mark.

Now the content words and the givens. Underline what the question is about: the iron three nitrate, and the change to a deeper red. Givens are usually there for a reason. For each one, ask what it tells you, then decide if your answer needs it. Iron three nitrate dissolves to give iron three plus ions, so a reactant goes up. And the temperature stays the same, so the collisions are no more energetic. Your answer is about how often the ions meet.

Last, the constraint: the phrase that tells you how to answer. Here it's "in terms of collision theory". In terms of means that idea must carry your explanation, so you'll talk about collisions and rates. Two other phrases turn up a lot. With reference to something means you name it and actually use it. Using the information means you take details from the stimulus, like numbers in a table, and say what they show.

So let's build the answer, in collision theory. If you take Biology, watch how each line uses the constraint. Adding iron three nitrate raises the concentration of iron three plus ions, so they collide with thiocyanate ions more often. That means more joining each second: the forward rate increases. That's the first point a marker can tick.

Now the link that makes it an explanation. The reverse reaction is the red ion splitting, which depends only on how many red ions there are. No extra red ions have formed yet, so the reverse rate hasn't changed. Forward is now faster than reverse, so red ions form faster than they split. That's point two. As red ions build up, the reverse rate rises and the forward rate falls, until the rates are equal again, with more red ion. That's why it's a deeper red. Three linked points, all in collision theory.

Now compare this answer. "Adding iron three plus ions increases a reactant, so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts right to use some of it up, and more of the red ion forms." Is it wrong? No, it's good chemistry. But it never mentions collisions or rates. It answers a nearby question: explain using Le Chatelier's principle. In our marking guide it earns one mark, for linking the shift to the deeper red.

So is it always one mark, one idea? As a rule of thumb, yes. A three-mark explain usually needs about three points. But it has limits. The points have to be linked, not just listed. Some marks need a specific thing, like a balanced equation or a value from the data. And longer answers are judged as a whole, so seven facts don't add up to seven marks.

Here's the routine. Ask four questions, in order. Do what? That's the verb. How much? That's the marks. About what? Those are the content words and givens. Using what? That's the constraint. It takes about thirty seconds. Then, when you've finished writing, go back and tick each part of the question your answer covers.

Your turn, with two questions. Do the one from your subject, or both. First, Biology. Roan cattle have a mix of red and white hairs. Roan cattle were crossed with each other, and the table shows their calves: 9 red, 21 roan and 10 white. Using the information provided, explain how these results show that roan cattle are heterozygous. Three marks. Run the routine, then answer. Pause here to answer.

The verb is explain, for three marks, and the constraint says use the data. So: roan parents had red calves and white calves, so each parent carries both alleles: heterozygous. Nine, twenty-one and ten is close to one to two to one, the ratio two heterozygous parents give. And roan calves are about half, the heterozygous share. The habit to drop: writing "codominance means both alleles show" and never using the numbers.

Now Chemistry. Colourless dinitrogen tetroxide forms brown nitrogen dioxide in a sealed flask, and the forward reaction is endothermic. The flask is placed in ice water. With reference to Le Chatelier's principle, predict and explain the change in colour. Three marks. Pause here to answer.

There are two verbs, so there are two jobs. Predict: the gas turns paler. Explain, and this time the constraint asks for Le Chatelier's principle, so name it. Cooling is the change, and the system partly counteracts it by favouring the reaction that gives out heat. That's the reverse reaction, so brown nitrogen dioxide turns into colourless dinitrogen tetroxide. The habit to drop: writing "it goes paler" and stopping. That's only one of the two jobs.

So before you write anything: do what, how much, about what, using what. Answer exactly that question, not the one next to it. Next: the verb that turns up more than any other in HSC science, explain, and how it differs from identify and describe.
